The word wrench has three distinct meanings as a noun. Think of them as three separate "lives" of the same word.

This is the most common meaning. A wrench is a hand tool — a device you grip in your hand and use manually — designed to turn nuts and bolts.

To understand why this tool exists, you first need to know what nuts and bolts are. They are small metal fasteners (joining pieces) used to hold things together — like parts of a car engine, a piece of furniture, or a bicycle. To tighten or loosen them, you need to rotate (turn) them. Your bare fingers are usually too weak to do this, especially when the bolt is stiff or very tight. A wrench solves this problem. It grips the nut or bolt firmly and gives you the leverage (mechanical advantage) to turn it with much greater force than your hand alone ever could.

The basic shape

Most wrenches have a handle (which you hold) and a head (the end that grips the nut or bolt). The head has an opening — either a gap or a socket — that fits around the nut or bolt.

Types of wrenches

There are several kinds, each designed for slightly different jobs:

  • Adjustable wrench — Its jaw (the gripping opening) can be made wider or narrower by turning a small screw mechanism on the head. This makes it versatile — one wrench can fit many different sizes of nuts and bolts. It is sometimes called a crescent wrench.
  • Open-end wrench — Has a fixed U-shaped opening at one or both ends. Because the size is fixed, you need a different wrench for each bolt size. It's fast to use because you don't need to place it over the bolt — you can slide it from the side.
  • Box-end wrench — Has a closed, ring-shaped opening that wraps completely around the bolt head. This gives a stronger, more secure grip than an open-end wrench.
  • Combination wrench — Has an open end on one side and a box end on the other, combining the benefits of both.
  • Socket wrench — Uses interchangeable sockets (small cup-shaped pieces) that fit over bolt heads. It often has a ratchet mechanism, meaning you can turn the bolt without lifting and repositioning the tool after each turn — you simply move the handle back and forth.
  • Allen wrench (hex key) — A small L-shaped rod, usually with a hexagonal (six-sided) cross-section. It is used for screws that have a six-sided hole in the center rather than a slot. Very commonly used in flat-pack furniture (like IKEA) and bicycles.
  • Torque wrench — A precision tool that measures exactly how much turning force (called torque) you are applying. Used when over-tightening or under-tightening a bolt would cause damage — for example, in car engines.
  • Pipe wrench — Has serrated, angled jaws designed to grip cylindrical objects like pipes. Used by plumbers.
  • Monkey wrench — An older-style adjustable wrench with a larger, heavier body. The term is also used informally to refer to adjustable wrenches in general.

A note for British English learners: In British English, what Americans call a "wrench" (the tool) is most commonly called a spanner. The word "wrench" is understood in British English but less common for the tool meaning.
Meaning 2: A Sudden, Violent Twist or Pull

A wrench can also refer to a sharp, forceful twisting or pulling movement applied to something — like when you yank something hard.

Examples:

  • "He gave the stuck lid a wrench and it finally came off."
  • "With a single wrench, she pulled the branch free from the tree."

Think of it as the action that a wrench tool performs — a forceful twist — now used as a word to describe that kind of movement in general.
Meaning 3: A Feeling of Emotional Pain or Distress

This is the most figurative (non-literal) meaning, and it is a very powerful one. A wrench refers to a sharp, deep feeling of pain, sadness, or loss — especially the kind you feel when you are parted from someone or something you love.

Imagine the physical sensation of something being pulled or twisted out of you. Now apply that image to your emotions. That is what this meaning captures — a kind of emotional tearing.

Examples:

  • "Leaving her hometown after twenty years was a real wrench."
  • "It was a terrible wrench to say goodbye to his closest friend."
  • "Giving away her late mother's belongings was a wrench she hadn't expected."

This meaning is often heard in phrases like "it was a wrench" or "a painful wrench."
A Common Phrase: "Throw a Wrench Into Something"

You will frequently come across this phrase, which comes directly from the tool meaning. To throw a wrench into something means to cause a disruption, complication, or problem that stops a plan or process from going smoothly.

It comes from the image of a wrench literally being thrown into a piece of running machinery — the machine would jam and break down.

Examples:

  • "The sudden rainstorm threw a wrench into their outdoor wedding plans."
  • "His resignation threw a wrench into the entire project."

In British English, the equivalent phrase is "throw a spanner in the works."

The toolA hand device used to grip and turn nuts, bolts, and pipes.
A movementA sudden, sharp twist or pull.
An emotionA feeling of deep pain or sadness, especially from separation or loss.
In a phraseThrow a wrench into something = cause a disruption or problem.
